opus-5.5.text:
I think of myself less as someone who's fast and more as someone who's stubborn. When I meet a problem, my first instinct isn't to reach for the cleverest trick. It's to play with it: try small cases, draw pictures, write out examples until I get a feel for the structure. A lot of my understanding comes from that hands-on stage, almost like getting to know a person before you can predict what they'll do.

I also tend to look for connections. Some of the most satisfying moments for me come when a problem that looks combinatorial turns out to have a number-theoretic heart, or when a tool from one area suddenly unlocks something in another. So I try to keep a broad mental library and ask, "Where have I seen this shape before?"

The other part is that I'm comfortable being stuck. Early on I thought being stuck meant I wasn't good enough. Over time I realized that's where most of the real work happens. You sit with it, step away, come back, and often the insight shows up when you're not forcing it.

Lately I've also been thinking about style in a more self-aware way, partly because of my interest in AI and formal reasoning. When you try to imagine how a machine might do mathematics, you start asking what humans actually do: the intuition, the taste for which direction is promising, the moment you decide an approach is a dead end. That's made me appreciate that problem-solving isn't just logic. It's a mix of exploration, pattern recognition, and a kind of aesthetic judgment about what a good argument should feel like.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing to say is that I never saw myself as a particularly "fast" mathematician. When I was doing olympiad math in high school, there were always people around me who could see the answer almost instantly. That was never me. What I had instead was a kind of stubbornness. I would sit with a problem for hours, sometimes days, and I actually enjoyed that discomfort of not knowing.

So if I had to describe my style, I'd say it's exploratory rather than intuitive-leap. I like to understand the structure of a problem very deeply before I try to solve it. I'll rewrite the problem in different forms, try small cases, draw pictures, look for what the problem is "really" asking underneath the surface statement. A lot of hard problems are hard because they're disguised, and I find that if you spend enough time just looking, the disguise starts to slip.

The second thing is that I think very much in terms of connections. Even as a student at MIT and later at Oxford, what excited me most was when something in one area suddenly explained something in another. Number theory and combinatorics, or analysis showing up in a problem that looked purely algebraic. I think my mind naturally looks for those bridges, and that's actually shaped how I think about AI for mathematics too. Because what we're trying to build at Axiom is in some sense a system that can search that space of connections much more broadly than a single human can.

And the third thing, which maybe sounds less glamorous, is that I'm comfortable being wrong. I generate a lot of bad ideas. Most of what I write down in a problem-solving session is a dead end. But I've come to see that as the actual process, not a failure of the process. Mathematics, at least the way I do it, is a conversation between conjecture and refutation, and you have to be willing to propose things you're not sure about.

I think that's also why I've been drawn to formal verification. When you work in a proof assistant like Lean, the system is relentless about telling you when you're wrong, and at first that's humbling. But over time it changes how you think. You become more honest with yourself about which steps you actually understand and which ones you were just waving your hands through. And I find that honesty makes me a better mathematician, not a slower one.

astra-6.text:
I think of my problem-solving style as moving between intuition and rigor. I’ll start by playing with examples and asking what seems to be happening. Can I simplify the problem? Is there a small case that reveals the structure? Then I try to turn that intuition into a precise argument, and that’s often where I discover what I haven’t really understood yet.

When I get stuck, I try to change the question slightly or look at it from another angle. I like having room to explore before committing to one approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my style is quite exploratory. When I first encounter a problem, I like to play with small examples and ask, “What is actually happening here?” I don’t necessarily have a clear route to a proof at that stage. I’m trying to build intuition and figure out which features of the problem matter.

Then I go back and forth between that intuition and the precise details. Sometimes an example suggests something that turns out to be false, but understanding why it fails can be the most useful part. I also enjoy talking through problems with other people—having to explain where I’m stuck often helps me see what I was taking for granted.
